Read the output

Source: vignettes/a05_output.Rmd
a05_output.Rmd

createTrajectories() returns a c2t_trajectories data frame and writes its rows to Data/patientDataDiscrete.csv or Data/patientDataContinuous.csv in the study folder.

Printing shows patient and state counts, boundary and unresolved-row counts, and a short preview. Every row and column remains available:

trajectories                  # Compact preview
print(trajectories, n = 10)    # Show more rows
as.data.frame(trajectories)   # Ordinary data-frame display

Columns

Column Meaning
subject_id The original patient identifier. Internal batching IDs are not exported.
episode_id Present only with targetEpisodeHandling = "All". Chronological target-period number within the patient, assigned before eligibility filtering.
state_label The selected clinical label, or START, EXIT or OUT OF COHORT.
state_start_date First date of the selected interval or discrete cycle.
state_end_date Last date of that interval or cycle, including this date.
time_in_cohort Years from the observation period’s start to this row’s start, calculated as elapsed days divided by 365.25.
seq_ordinal Consecutive occurrence number of the same label in that patient’s output rows. It resets when the label changes. It is not a cycle number.
state_id An identifier assigned to the label within the run. It is not a clinical concept ID or a cross-database key.
age Age in years at this row’s start, when a CDM demographic join is used. Otherwise NA.
gender_concept_id The CDM person’s recorded gender concept ID, when joined. Otherwise NA.
state_key Present only for merged studies. Identifies the original members of a state across runs with the same labels.

In "All" mode, START, EXIT, cycles, time_in_cohort and seq_ordinal restart in each episode. Use both subject_id and episode_id to identify a history. State IDs and the state dictionary cover the whole study. No rows represent the gaps between episodes.

Dates are Date values in R and date strings in CSV. Use column names rather than positions. Treat state_id as an identifier; its type can be character or numeric. Inspect unmerged IDs with unique(trajectories[c("state_id", "state_label")]).

When reading a CSV, preserve patient identifiers as text:

trajectories <- read.csv(
  "MyStudy/Data/patientDataDiscrete.csv",
  colClasses = "character",
  na.strings = NULL
)
trajectories$state_start_date <- as.Date(trajectories$state_start_date)
trajectories$state_end_date <- as.Date(trajectories$state_end_date)
for (column in c("time_in_cohort", "seq_ordinal", "age", "gender_concept_id")) {
  trajectories[[column]] <- type.convert(trajectories[[column]], as.is = TRUE)
}

This preserves leading zeros, long identifiers and literal labels such as "NA", then converts known numeric columns. Supply large in-memory input IDs as character or integer64; digits rounded by numeric storage cannot be recovered.

Observation boundaries and unresolved cycles

By default, the first target interval supplies observation bounds. A selected absorbing state can end follow-up early; outOfCohortAllowed = TRUE lets retained records extend its end, but not its start. With targetEpisodeHandling = "All", every episode has its own target bounds and outOfCohortAllowed must be FALSE. Later episodes remain eligible after absorption unless stopAfterAbsorbingEpisode = TRUE.

START marks the first date. EXIT is the day after the retained follow-up endpoint: the final cycle end for discrete output. Each marker has identical start and end dates and contributes no observed days. Exclude them when estimating time spent in clinical states.

OUT OF COHORT is a discrete cycle with no selected state, within observation. Deleting these rows can make separated states look adjacent. Decide how to handle them before estimating transitions.

Discrete dates are cycle dates

With cycleLength = 7, a cycle beginning January 1 ends January 7. The next begins January 8. If observation ends January 10, that final cycle contains three observed days. For non-marker rows, duration is as.integer(state_end_date - state_start_date) + 1.

One label represents the whole cycle. Its dates need not match the selected event’s dates. A selected absorbing state stops generation after its cycle. Absorption does not shorten that cycle to the event date; an observation boundary on that date does.

History-specific death states can preserve a prior complication category, but not its exact date within the cycle. See the weekly example.

Continuous dates are interval dates

Continuous output retains selected interval endpoints, subject to observation and absorbing-state rules. Gaps remain unfilled and simultaneous records keep their dates. Priority can split intervals; First and Overlap can retain overlaps. Summing overlapping lengths overcounts patient-time. Models requiring one state at every instant need an explicit rule for these overlaps.

State membership

For merged studies, study$stateDictionary and Data/stateDictionary.rds describe each original or combined state:

Field Meaning
state_key Stable key built from the original member labels.
label Display label used in the trajectory.
members List of original state labels.
absorbing Whether selecting this state ends the trajectory.
allowedTransitions List of permitted destination keys.
state_id Run-local ID, added during generation.

Use members to inspect a combination. Do not split its display label or key. The dictionary does not include boundary or unresolved-gap markers. Unmerged studies do not produce this dictionary.

Files to keep

File Purpose
Settings/analysisSettings.rds Completed import and generation rules. For CDM studies it also contains the cohort JSON definitions used during import.
Data/patientDataDiscrete.csv or Data/patientDataContinuous.csv Patient trajectories.
Data/importedDataCleaned.csv Intervals used as input to trajectory generation. The filename is independent of the cohort-definition path.
Data/sourceIntervals.rds Merged studies only. Cleaned intervals before overlapping states were combined.
Data/stateDictionary.rds Merged studies only. Membership and resolved state rules.

The interval files reflect observation limits, mandatory-state requirements and combined overlapping records of the same state. In merged studies, sourceIntervals.rds retains the original state labels before composition.

Settings store import and generation separately. For example, after settings <- readRDS("MyStudy/Settings/analysisSettings.rds"), the cycle length is settings$generation$cycleLength. See Import cohort data for saved-study setup and format compatibility.

Share Settings to reproduce the rules. CDM settings include cohort definitions; no settings file contains patient records or a database connection. Data contains patient-level records.

Handing the result to an analysis package

The trajectory_definition attribute records the format version, effective trajectory type, cycle length, ordered clinical labels and absorbing labels. Labels and absorbing status reflect merged-state overrides; configured states remain declared when absent from the data. Inspect it with attr(trajectories, "trajectory_definition").

For default "First" output, TMA reads the version-1 definition directly:

histories <- TrajectoryMarkovAnalysis::prepareTrajectories(trajectories)
transitions <- TrajectoryMarkovAnalysis::estimateTransitions(histories)

"All" output uses a version-2 definition to mark its separate episodes. The current TMA reader accepts only version 1 and rejects this output. An analysis must preserve episode boundaries rather than joining the end of one episode to the start of the next. Removing the attribute does not make such a join valid.

Use saveRDS(trajectories, "trajectories.rds") to preserve rows and definitions. Ordinary data-frame row subsets also retain the attribute. CSV preserves only rows. For "First" CSVs, supply cycle length, state labels and absorbing states to TMA explicitly. TMA rejects settings conflicting with an attached definition. Update the definition if a transformation changes state meanings or cycle length.

Keep the separate state dictionary for merged membership. The handoff contains labels and absorbing status, rather than the full selection and transition rules.

Cohort2Trajectory constructs histories; downstream packages estimate transitions, effects and costs. Check their treatment of boundaries, gaps, overlaps and short final cycles. Exact event-time analyses need interval dates rather than weekly cycle dates.
